scenes.name: Nueva psicodelia y big music: Echo & the Bunnymen y U2
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: En lugar de descender a lo oscuro, elevarse hacia la luz. Liverpool, que no tuvo punk clásico ni postpunk experimental, quería que la música fuera «una fiesta» (Bill Drummond, Zoo): el club Eric's, las bandas fantasma (The Crucial Three, Big in Japan), Wah! Heat, The Teardrop Explodes de Julian Cope. Echo & the Bunnymen, con el minimalismo aprendido de Television y la voz de Ian McCulloch, graban Crocodiles y Heaven Up Here, respuesta luminosa a Closer, y heredan el público huérfano de Joy Division; Ocean Rain los vuelve estrellas pop. U2, «punk positivo» cristiano y pacifista, guitarra de The Edge como sintetizador, quiere ocupar el lugar de Curtis: War (1983), «Sunday Bloody Sunday» en MTV, The Unforgettable Fire con Eno. Alrededor, la «big music» celta de Simple Minds, The Waterboys, Big Country y la neopsicodelia de The Blue Orchids.

podcast.title: Alleged Quit Threat Post-Live Aid (July 13, 1985)
podcast.body: Following a heated argument backstage after U2's Live Aid set, Bono allegedly told the band, "fine, I quit," expressing his frustration with the situation. "Emotions got out of control, and Bono allegedly said, fine, I quit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1

podcast.title: Grandstanding at Live Aid (July 13, 1985)
podcast.body: During U2's performance of "Bad" at Live Aid, Bono engaged in an extended moment trying to pull a dance partner from the audience, consuming many minutes of their allotted time. This "grandstanding" caused the band to miss playing their biggest hit, "Pride (In the Name of Love)," and led to a major backstage confrontation. "Donald decided he needed a dance partner and spent many long minutes trying to pull somebody out of the audience."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1

podcast.title: Reconsideration and Apology After Live Aid (July 13, 1985)
podcast.body: After allegedly quitting U2 following Live Aid, Bono flew back to Dublin alone and took a long drive to calm down. During this drive, he reportedly picked up a female hitchhiker who recognized him and praised U2's performance. This conversation prompted Bono to reconsider his decision, leading him to apologize to the other band members in Dublin and ask to be allowed back into the group. "This conversation made Bono think that maybe he had been a little hasty in quitting."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1

podcast.title: Jamaican Shooting Incident (1996)
podcast.body: On January 16, 1996, Bono, his family, and friends including Jimmy Buffett and Island Records head Chris Blackwell, were taxing on the tarmac at Negril airport in Jamaica aboard Buffett's Grumman HU-16C plane, "Hemisphere Dancer," with Buffett at the controls. Jamaican police mistakenly believed the aircraft was a drug runner's plane and opened fire on it. Bono described the terrifying event as being "in the middle of a James Bond movie," and while everyone was safe, he and his family cut their holiday short, spending the rest of their time in Miami, with the Jamaican government issuing a full apology. "Those boys were shooting all over the place. I felt as if we were in the middle of a James Bond movie. Only this was real."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Character Witness for Peter Buck (April 5, 2002)
podcast.body: Bono testified as a character witness for R.E.M. guitarist Peter Buck during his second trial on charges of air rage. Buck was eventually acquitted, largely due to a medical defense of "non-insane automatism." "Bono of you two testifying as a character witness."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1

podcast.title: 360 Tour Postponement and Financial Impact (2010)
podcast.body: Due to Bono's back injury, 16 scheduled North American dates on U2's massive 360 world tour had to be postponed for a year. This resulted in an estimated loss of $100 million in ticket sales, marking the largest insurance claim in the history of canceled concerts. "The 16 canceled dates represented a loss of about $100 million in ticket sales. It was the biggest insurance claim in the history of canceled concerts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Back Injury and Emergency Surgery (May 10, 2010)
podcast.body: On his 50th birthday, Bono experienced severe back pain, followed by leg numbness and partial paralysis. He was rushed for emergency surgery, where he was diagnosed with a herniated disc, severe compression of the sciatic nerve, an 8-millimeter tear in the disc's ligaments, and disc fragments in his spinal canal. Delicate surgery was required to prevent permanent paralysis. "He was rushed to the hospital for emergency surgery. The problem was discovered to be a herniated disc and a severe compression of the sciatic nerve."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Munich Clinic Recovery (2010)
podcast.body: After his initial back surgery, Bono was sent to a clinic in Munich for recovery. He recovered well, joking about being "rebuilt by German engineering." The tour was able to resume in Italy that August. "After the initial surgery, he was sent to a clinic in Munich."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bicycle Crash and Multiple Fractures (November 2014)
podcast.body: While preparing for the Innocence and Experience tour, Bono crashed his bike in Central Park, sustaining severe injuries. These included a left facial fracture (affecting his eye orbit), a left scapula (shoulder blade) fractured in three places, a left compound distal humerus fracture (where the bone broke in six pieces and pierced his skin), and a fracture of his fifth metacarpal in his left hand. "He was riding his bike through Central Park and he crashed. Hard. And the injuries were ugly."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Extensive Arm and Hand Surgery (November 2014)
podcast.body: The bicycle crash necessitated five hours of surgery to repair his arm, where a nerve was moved, and the bone was fixed with three metal plates and 18 screws. Additional surgery was required for his fractured left hand. "There was five hours of surgery where the album [likely 'arm'] was washed out and reset. A nerve trapped in the break was moved and the bone was repaired with three metal plates and 18 screws."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Learjet Cargo Hatch Detachment (2014)
podcast.body: On November 13, 2014, while Bono was on a two-hour flight from Dublin to Berlin's Schönefeld Airport aboard a private Learjet 60, the rear cargo hatch of the plane became detached as it approached the German coast. Passengers heard a "big thud," and at 12:15 AM, 11 minutes before touchdown, the door blew off entirely. Upon landing, two suitcases were found missing, and a piece of the door was later discovered in the Brandenburg area. "As the plane approached the German coast, the rear cargo hatch of the plane became detached."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lingering Guitar Playing Difficulty (2014 onwards)
podcast.body: Following his extensive arm and hand injuries, Bono still lacked feeling in two fingers and expressed concern that doctors believed he might never play the guitar properly again due to the inability to form chords with all his fingers. "I still don't have any feeling in two fingers. Doctors say I might never play the guitar properly again because I can't use all my fingers to form chords."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Arm and Back Injuries
podcast.body: Bono has sustained a significant "bum left arm" from a severe bicycle accident in New York's Central Park. Additionally, he has struggled with a back condition that nearly resulted in paralysis and necessitated extensive, complex surgery. "That's in addition to a back condition that nearly left him paralyzed and required all sorts of complicated surgery."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cited as a Rock Poet
podcast.body: Bono is listed as one of the rare "poets in rock," alongside other prominent lyricists. "There's Dylan, Springsteen, Patty Smith, Jim Morrison, Bono, certainly, maybe Lou Reed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Debunked "Hassidic Jew" Crash Story
podcast.body: A rumor circulated that Bono was dressed as a Hassidic Jew when he crashed his bike. The Edge clarified this was a joke he had made in a radio interview, suggesting it as a reason why Bono might not have been recognized, and confirmed it was not true. "He told me that when Bono crashed his bike, he was dressed as a hersteaded Jew. That was a joke and I'm responsible for it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Glaucoma Diagnosis and Sunglasses (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: Bono was diagnosed with glaucoma, a chronic eye condition that causes pressure buildup on the eyeball, in the early 1990s. One of its symptoms is sensitivity to light, even indoors, which is the medical reason he started wearing sunglasses consistently around that time. He has undergone various treatments like eye drops and lasers to prevent optic nerve damage. "Bono was first diagnosed with Glacoma in the early 1990s, which, as you might remember, is exactly when he started wearing sunglasses all the time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inspiration from Greg Carroll for "The Joshua Tree"
podcast.body: Following the death of U2 roadie Greg Carroll, Bono, while working on lyrics for "The Joshua Tree" album, recalled a tour of Auckland given to him by Carroll. This experience, particularly a visit to the sacred Maori site of Maungakiekie (One Tree Hill), became a direct lyrical inspiration for the album and the song "One Tree Hill," both dedicated to Carroll. "When everyone returned to Ireland, Bono, who was working on lyrics for songs for what would become the Joshua Tree album, remembered that tour of Auckland that he got from Carroll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: We Are The Road Crew - A History of Roadies

podcast.title: Musical Parent
podcast.body: Paul Husson, known as Bono, is the father of Eli Husson, who fronted the band Inhaler. "Paul Husson, better known as Bono."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Passion Rooted in Mother's Death
podcast.body: Much of Bono's passion is believed to be rooted in the events surrounding his mother's death when he was still a teenager. "Bono's passion is rooted in everything that happened to him when his mother died when he was still in his teens."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Performance at Greg Carroll's Funeral
podcast.body: At the funeral service for U2 roadie Greg Carroll, "Carroll" sang "Let It Be" and "Knockin' on Heaven's Door." While the transcript states "Carroll sang," it is likely a reference to Bono or another U2 member performing, given the context of U2's presence at the funeral. "Members of U2 went to the funeral. Carroll sang Let It Be and Knock on Unheaven's Door at the ceremony."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: We Are The Road Crew - A History of Roadies

podcast.title: Political Leader Archetype
podcast.body: Bono is identified as a quintessential political leader within a band, focused on strategic and economic decisions rather than purely creative ones, alongside Mick Jagger. "líderes políticos tenemos, yo creo que por excelencia son bono dentro de YouTube."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Rare Trapdoor Spider Species
podcast.body: A trapdoor spider, *Apthostica's Bonoai*, was named after Bono. This species is exceptionally rare, with only a single male and female pair ever discovered, and it is native to the Joshua Tree National Forest, establishing a direct link to U2's famous album. "It is called Apthostica's Bonoai. After Bono, of course, in the whole Joshua Tree Island."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Recognition of "Bombast" in Arcade Fire
podcast.body: Bono, lead singer of U2, recognized a similar kind of "bombast" in Arcade Fire's music and artistry that he believed had contributed to U2's own early fame. "Same with Bono, who sees in them the same kind of bombass that made you two famous back in the day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Who the Hell is Arcade Fire? Part 2

podcast.title: Spiritual Advisor on Tour
podcast.body: Bono frequently toured with his own full-time priest and spiritual advisor, Reverend Jack Heeslip. Heeslip initially met U2 when he was a teacher and counselor at Mount Temple High School in Dublin, where the band members were students. Reverend Jack passed away in 2015. "Bono often used to tour with his own full-time priest and spiritual advisor, a guy named Reverend Jack Heeslip."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 60 Mind-Blowing Facts About Music in 60 Minutes: 2017 Edition

podcast.title: Time Change Disorientation in Auckland
podcast.body: Upon arriving in Auckland in 1984 for U2's "Unforgettable Fire" tour, Bono was "completely out of sorts" due to the time changes. During this period, he took a tour of the city with local roadie Greg Carroll, an experience that later deeply inspired his songwriting. "When they arrived, Bono, completely out of sorts because of the time changes, went for a tour of Auckland. And with him was a guy named Greg Carroll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: We Are The Road Crew - A History of Roadies

podcast.title: Unique Award Nominations Achievement
podcast.body: Bono holds the distinction of being the only individual to have been nominated for a Grammy, a Golden Globe, an Oscar, and a Nobel Peace Prize, recognizing his wide-ranging achievements in music, film, and humanitarian efforts. "Can you name the only person to be nominated for a Grammy, a Golden Globe, an Oscar and Nobel Peace Prize? Bono."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Vocal Preservation
podcast.body: Bono is noted for doing an excellent job maintaining his voice in shape and being very careful with his instrument. Despite this, he has adapted his live performances of U2 songs in recent years, often lowering the key of songs like "Beautiful Day" to accommodate vocal changes. "Bono has done an excellent job in keeping his voice in shape. He's very careful with his instrument."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
